2.text: quantity of food. We paid for food with compressed tea and leaf-tobacco in

3.text: very moderate proportion, as is usually done in such cases. Čaˊnla, however,

4.text: wanted no tea or tobacco. He wanted to buy the leader of one of our dog-

5.text: teams, a white female, uncommonly large, whose name was Arrow. Russian

6.text: dogs are highly valued among the Maritime Chukchee. In payment for the

7.text: dog, he offered a beaver-skin, two fox-skins, and this bag of blubber. The

8.text: peltries were not as yet in his possession; but he intended to acquire them

9.text: in the course of the summer from the Alaskan Eskimo traders, and promised

10.text: to deliver them on our return journey in a couple of months or so. The owner

11.text: of the dog, who was one of my Cossacks, refused to sell it on credit. Then

12.text: Čaˊnla, offended at this lack of confidence in him, took back his bag and

13.text: returned to his home. Shortly afterward it appeared that we could not buy any

14.text: other food in that village. “Čaˊnla is the eˊrmečɪn,” explained the inhabitants,

15.text: “and he says ‘no traffic!’” So our dogs had but a scanty meal, given by

16.text: the master of the house we stopped in. In the end we had to yield; and the

17.text: dog was handed over to Čaˊnla, who, by the way, in due time faithfully delivered

19.text: We took the bag with blubber, and also a quantity of walrus-meat from

20.text: the other inhabitants, and everything was smoothed over. When I asked some

21.text: of the people afterwards whether the word of Čaˊnla was really of such weight

22.text: with them, they answered, “He is our neighbor and a great wrestler.” Čaˊnla

23.text: was not yet thirty. He was tall of stature and strongly built. He wore

24.text: breeches adorned all over with red tassels,¹ and held himself always ready for

25.text: a wrestling-match. The house we stopped in was the “front house;” and the

26.text: master of it was richer than Čaˊnla, though the influence of Čaˊnla seemed to

27.text: be greater among the inhabitants. I should mention, however, that in the

28.text: Maritime villages, as a usual thing, the strongest man is also the richest,

29.text: because, on account of his physical resources, he is more successful in hunting

30.text: than others. Moreover, the front-house family is generally the strongest and the

31.text: richest, and its head plays the eˊrmečɪn among the other people. From this

32.text: also sprang the maritime term for the front house, aˊrmačɪ-raˊn (“the house

33.text: of the strongest”). Among the Reindeer Chukchee, wealth in reindeer does

34.text: not depend so much on physical strength, and there are cases where the

35.text: “strongest man” is also the poorest, as will be shown presently.

36.text: “VIOLENT MEN.” — In the sense of “violent man,” “robber,” the term

37.text: “eˊrmečɪn” is used as much by the Reindeer Chukchee as by the Maritime;

38.text: but as to the social position of the “violent men,” I would call attention to

39.text: a very interesting difference between both branches of the tribe.

41.text: is the poor assistant, who uses his physical advantages as means of violence
